title: Cardinal Points of a Coaxial Optical System
short_intro: A coaxial optical system comprising multiple refracting surfaces can be completely characterized by six cardinal points situated on its principal axis. These points include two focal points, two principal points, and two nodal points.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic definitions and properties of principal foci and principal planes for thick lenses and coaxial systems.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed analytical derivation of focal lengths, positions of principal and nodal points, and Newton's formula using matrix methods and cardinal point relations.

prerequisites: Laws of refraction and paraxial approximation (Snell's law)
Matrix method in geometrical optics (System matrix / ABCD matrix)
Refraction through a single spherical surface and thick lenses

concept_notes.heading: Introduction to Cardinal Points
bullets: A coaxial system of centring lenses and spherical refracting surfaces has six designated cardinal points on its principal axis.
These points consist of three pairs: two principal foci (F<sub>1</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>), two principal points (H<sub>1</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>), and two nodal points (N<sub>1</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>).
Knowing these points allows any complex optical system to be treated as a 'black box', simplifying ray tracing and image formation calculations.

concept_notes.heading: Principal Foci (F<sub>1</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>)
bullets: The first focal point (F<sub>1</sub>) or object focus is an axial point for which rays starting from it emerge parallel to the principal axis after refraction.
The second focal point (F<sub>2</sub>) or image focus is an axial point where rays parallel to the principal axis incident on the system converge or appear to diverge from after refraction.

The distance from the first principal point to F<sub>1</sub> is the first focal length (f<sub>1</sub>), and from the second principal point to F<sub>2</sub> is the second focal length (f<sub>2</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Principal Planes and Points (H<sub>1</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>)
bullets: Principal planes are a pair of conjugate planes on the optical axis for which the transverse magnification is +1.
This implies that an object of height y placed in the first principal plane forms an erect image of the same height y in the second principal plane.
The points of intersection of these planes with the principal axis are called the principal points (H<sub>1</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>).

concept_notes.heading: Nodal Points and Optical Center (N<sub>1</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>)
bullets: Nodal points are a pair of conjugate points on the axis having an angular magnification of +1.
A ray directed toward the first nodal point (N<sub>1</sub>) emerges from the second nodal point (N<sub>2</sub>) parallel to its initial direction.
If the medium on both sides of the optical system is the same, the nodal points coincide with the principal points.

derivations.title: Relation between Focal Lengths and Refractive Indices
derivations.conditions: Coaxial system bounded by refractive indices mu_1 on the object side and mu_2 on the image side.
steps: Consider paraxial rays traveling from a medium of refractive index mu_1 to mu_2 through the optical system.
Using Lagrange's invariant or the refraction matrix elements (A, B, C, D) for the system, relate object and image coordinates.
Apply the condition for principal foci where parallel incident rays yield a focus, and vice versa.
Express the ratio of focal lengths in terms of the terminal refractive indices.

derivations.title: Newton's Optical Formula for Cardinal Points
derivations.conditions: Distances measured from the respective principal foci.
steps: Let x_1 be the distance of the object from the first principal focus F_1, and x_2 be the distance of the image from the second principal focus F_2.
Using the linear magnification equations referenced to the principal foci, write x_1 and x_2.
Multiply the distances x_1 and x_2 to find the constant product relation.

formula_sheet.name: Newton's Formula
formula_sheet.variables: x_1 = object distance from F_1, x_2 = image distance from F_2, f_1, f_2 = focal lengths

formula_sheet.name: Ratio of Focal Lengths
formula_sheet.variables: f_1, f_2 = focal lengths, \mu_1, \mu_2 = initial and final refractive indices
formula_sheet.conditions: General coaxial system in different media

formula_sheet.name: Transverse Magnification at Principal Planes
formula_sheet.variables: h_1 = object height, h_2 = image height
formula_sheet.conditions: At principal planes H_1 and H_2

formula_sheet.name: System Matrix (ABCD Matrix)
formula_sheet.equation_html: \begin{pmatrix} \mu_2 \sin u_2 \\ y_2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \mu_1 \sin u_1 \\ y_1 \end{pmatrix}
formula_sheet.variables: A, B, C, D = system matrix elements, y = heights, u = angles

formula_sheet.name: Power of the Optical System
formula_sheet.variables: P = optical power, f_1, f_2 = focal lengths, \mu_1, \mu_2 = refractive indices

formula_sheet.name: Position of First Principal Point from First Surface
formula_sheet.variables: C, D = elements of the refraction matrix from the first surface to the system boundary

formula_sheet.name: Position of Second Principal Point from Last Surface
formula_sheet.variables: A, C = elements of the system matrix

formula_sheet.name: Nodal Point Separation from Principal Points
formula_sheet.variables: H_1, H_2 = principal points, N_1, N_2 = nodal points

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ray Tracing through Cardinal Points
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A thick lens or black-box coaxial system showing principal planes H_1, H_2, foci F_1, F_2, and incident/emergent paraxial rays bending at the principal planes.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates that refraction can be treated as occurring instantaneously at the principal planes H_1 and H_2.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual diagram matching and identifying conjugate planes.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Newton's Graphical Verification
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_graph: Plot of image distance x_2 versus object distance x_1 measured from respective foci, showing a hyperbola.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the inverse relationship x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in advanced practical optics and numerical evaluation questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnification versus Object Position
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_graph: Transverse magnification m plotted against object distance from the first focal point.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows how magnification varies hyperbolically around the focal points.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tests understanding of conjugate points and scale factors.

solved_numericals.question: The focal lengths of a coaxial optical system in air are given as f_1 = -15 cm and f_2 = +15 cm. Find the optical power of the system.
solution_steps: Identify the medium: since it is in air, \mu_1 = \mu_2 = 1.
Use the power formula P = \frac{1}{f_2} (in meters).
Substitute f_2 = +0.15 m into the formula.

solved_numericals.question: For a coaxial optical system separating two media with \mu_1 = 1.0 and \mu_2 = 1.5, the first focal length f_1 is -10 cm. Determine the second focal length f_2.
solution_steps: Recall the relation between focal lengths and refractive indices: \frac{f_1}{f_2} = -\frac{\mu_1}{\mu_2}.
Rearrange to solve for f_2: f_2 = -f_1 \left(\frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\right).
Substitute the given values: f_2 = -(-10 \text{ cm}) \left(\frac{1.5}{1.0}\right).
Calculate the final value: f_2 = 10 \times 1.5 = +15 \text{ cm}.

solved_numericals.question: In a coaxial system, an object placed 5 cm from the first principal focus F_1 forms an image at a distance of 20 cm from the second principal focus F_2. Find the product of the focal lengths f_1 f_2.
solution_steps: Use Newton's optical formula: x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2.
Substitute the given distances from the foci: x_1 = 5 \text{ cm} and x_2 = 20 \text{ cm}.
Calculate the product: f_1 f_2 = 5 \times 20 = 100 \text{ cm}^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: Paraxial approximation (sin \theta \approx \theta, \tan \theta \approx \theta) must hold valid for all rays.
The system is assumed to be strictly coaxial with spherical refracting surfaces.
Apertures are assumed small to avoid spherical and chromatic aberrations affecting cardinal point locations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Principal points are always located inside the physical boundaries of the lenses.
common_misconceptions.correct: Principal points can lie outside the lens system, depending on the curvatures and separation of the component lenses.
common_misconceptions.why: The principal planes are mathematical constructs defined by unit magnification, not physical surfaces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Nodal points and principal points are always at the exact same positions.
common_misconceptions.correct: They coincide only when the refractive index of the medium on the object side equals that of the image side.
common_misconceptions.why: When \mu_1 \neq \mu_2, the separation between principal points and nodal points depends on the ratio of the refractive indices and focal lengths.

quick_revision: A coaxial system has exactly 6 cardinal points: 2 foci, 2 principal points, and 2 nodal points.
Principal planes have a transverse magnification of +1.
Newton's formula is given by x_1 x_2 = f_1 f_2.
The ratio of focal lengths satisfies f_1 / f_2 = - \mu_1 / \mu_2.
